sets.title: LEDs
sets.blurb: Light up addressable LED strips with an ESP32, and fix the things that go wrong on the way.

sets.title: ESP32-C3
sets.blurb: The tiny board we use most: buttons, pins, power, WiFi and Bluetooth, and how to get code onto it.

sets.title: Multimeter
sets.blurb: Plug in the probes, then check continuity, volts and amps without blowing a fuse.

sets.title: Soldering
sets.blurb: The right solder, the right temperature, and joints that hold.

sets.title: Components
sets.blurb: Resistors, capacitors, LEDs, transistors and MOSFETs: what each part does and how to pick the right one.

sets.title: Raspberry Pi
sets.blurb: Setting up a Raspberry Pi without a screen, keeping it powered and its SD card healthy, and the projects we run on them: a streaming speaker and RGB LED panels.

workshopGuides.title: Programming LEDs
workshopGuides.hook: Flash an ESP32-C3, light up an LED strip, then change the code and make it do something new.

topics.title: How one wire drives a whole strip of LEDs
topics.hook: No LED on the strip has an address. So how does LED 7 know which color is its?
topics.post: No LED on an addressable strip has an address. Watch how one wire tells a whole strip what to do, and the ways it fails silently.

topics.title: Why delay() makes your project ignore you
topics.hook: Press the button. The board with delay() will miss most of your presses.
topics.post: Press the button. The board using delay() misses most presses. The one using millis() never does. A 3-minute interactive explainer.

topics.title: Baud rate: why your serial monitor shows garbage
topics.hook: "­¾ýÿ¿þ" in your serial monitor is good news: the wiring works, only the speed is wrong.
topics.description: Garbage characters in your serial monitor are good news: the wiring works, only the speed is wrong.
topics.post: Garbage characters in your serial monitor? Your wiring is probably fine. See exactly why a baud-rate mismatch scrambles text, with a live decoder.

topics.title: The USB cable that looks fine and isn’t
topics.hook: The board lights up, but your laptop can’t see it. It’s probably the cable.
topics.post: Board lights up but your computer can’t see it? Charge-only USB cables look identical to data cables. See what’s missing inside.

topics.title: How many LEDs can USB power?
topics.hook: A ten-LED strip on full white can draw more than a USB port supplies, and the board starts rebooting.
topics.post: Why does my LED strip keep rebooting the board on white? An interactive look at how much current LEDs draw, and how much USB can give.

topics.title: ESP32-C3 SuperMini pinout, explained
topics.hook: Sixteen pins, a few with surprises. Tap any pin to see what it does.
topics.post: An interactive pinout for the tiny ESP32-C3 SuperMini: tap any pin to see what it does, including the three that can stop your board from booting.

topics.title: Multimeter probes: which jack is which
topics.hook: Black goes in COM. Red goes in V almost every time. The jacks marked A are the ones that blow fuses.
topics.post: Black probe, red probe, three or four jacks with tiny labels. Click to plug them in and find out which jack is which, and which one blows fuses.

topics.title: Continuity: is this wire actually connected?
topics.hook: Touch the probes to both ends of a wire. A beep means it’s connected. Silence means it isn’t.
topics.post: Is this wire actually connected? The multimeter’s beep setting answers in a second. Try it on a good wire, a broken one and a switch.

topics.title: Measuring voltage with a multimeter
topics.hook: Check a battery, then the 5V and 3.3 pins on your board. And find out what the minus sign means.
topics.post: Measure a battery and your ESP32 board’s 5V and 3.3V pins with a multimeter, and learn what a minus sign or a lone 1 on the display means.

topics.title: Measuring current without blowing the fuse
topics.hook: To measure current the meter goes in the circuit, not across it. Put it across a battery and the fuse blows.
topics.post: Measuring current is the one multimeter job that blows fuses. See why the meter goes in the circuit, not across it, and measure an LED’s 18 mA.

topics.title: Which solder wire should you buy?
topics.hook: Leaded or lead-free, thick or thin, and the one kind that must never touch a circuit board.
topics.post: Leaded or lead-free? 0.8 mm or 1.6 mm? And why plumbing solder ruins circuit boards. A quick, interactive guide to picking solder wire for electronics.

topics.title: What temperature should your soldering iron be?
topics.hook: Too cold makes a dull, weak joint. Too hot burns the flux and lifts the pad. Find the window.
topics.post: Too cold gives a dull, grainy joint. Too hot burns the flux and lifts pads. Turn the dial and find the window for leaded and lead-free solder, and see why tip size matters.

topics.title: Tin first, then join
topics.hook: Two surfaces already coated in solder flow together in a second. Bare ones fight you.
topics.post: The trick that makes soldering wires easy: tin the wire, tin the pad, then join them. Try it both ways and compare.

topics.title: Spot the bad solder joint
topics.hook: A good joint looks like a tiny shiny volcano. Can you name what went wrong with the others?
topics.post: Cold, dry, bridged, blobbed or cooked? A quick quiz: spot the bad solder joint, then learn what caused it and how to fix it.

topics.title: Why your soldering tip stopped working
topics.hook: A black tip won’t take solder, however hot it is. Here’s how it got that way, and how to keep it shiny.
topics.post: A black soldering tip won’t take solder, however hot you run it. See what oxidizes a tip, and the two habits that keep it shiny for years.

topics.title: Soldering header pins onto the ESP32-C3 SuperMini
topics.hook: Use a breadboard as a jig, tack two opposite corners, and the pins come out straight every time.
topics.post: Straight header pins on the first try: use a breadboard as a jig and tack two opposite corners first. A step-by-step guide for the ESP32-C3 SuperMini.

topics.title: The BOOT and RESET buttons on the ESP32-C3
topics.hook: Hold BOOT, tap RESET, let go of BOOT. It rescues a board that won’t take new code.
topics.post: Two tiny buttons on the ESP32-C3 SuperMini: RESET restarts your code, and BOOT + RESET puts the board in download mode. Try the sequence on a live board.

topics.title: When your ESP32-C3 won’t upload
topics.hook: No port, the wrong port, a busy port, or a board too busy to listen. Answer a few questions and find the fix.
topics.post: ESP32-C3 won’t take your code? Answer a few yes/no questions and get the fix: cable, port, serial monitor, or download mode.

topics.title: Where did my Serial output go?
topics.hook: Your code prints, the monitor stays blank. On an ESP32-C3, two missing lines in platformio.ini send it all to pin 21.
topics.post: Serial.println() on an ESP32-C3 and a blank monitor? Two build flags decide whether output goes over USB or out of pin 21. See both, live.

topics.title: Your first PlatformIO project for the ESP32-C3
topics.hook: A few lines of platformio.ini get you building. Tap each one to see what it does, and what breaks if it’s wrong.
topics.post: A platformio.ini for the ESP32-C3 SuperMini, one line at a time. Change a line and see what breaks: wrong board, wrong framework, missing USB flags.

topics.title: The pins that can stop your ESP32-C3 from booting
topics.hook: Wire a button to the wrong pin and your board sits waiting for new code instead of running yours.
topics.post: Wire a button to the wrong pin and your ESP32-C3 never runs your program. Meet the three strapping pins, 2, 8 and 9, and test what boots.

topics.title: Which ESP32-C3 pins are safe to use?
topics.hook: Some pins already have a second job: USB, serial, the flash chip. Pick a job and see which pins are free.
topics.post: Some ESP32-C3 pins already have a second job: USB, serial, the flash chip, booting. Pick a job, like a button or an analog sensor, and see which SuperMini pins are safe.

topics.title: Reading analog voltages on the ESP32-C3
topics.hook: analogRead() gives a number from 0 to 4095, but it’s noisy and stops being accurate above about 2.5 V.
topics.post: The ESP32-C3 reads voltages from 0 to 4095, but the numbers are noisy and top out around 2.5 V. Slide the voltage, average the noise, and size a divider for a battery.

topics.title: Fading an LED with PWM on the ESP32-C3
topics.hook: The pin is only ever on or off. Switch it fast enough and the LED looks dimmed.
topics.post: An ESP32-C3 pin is only ever on or off, yet it can fade an LED. Drag the duty cycle, watch the wave, and see why half duty doesn’t look half as bright.

topics.title: Powering the ESP32-C3 without USB
topics.hook: Batteries, power banks, the 5V pin or the 3.3 pin: which ones are safe, and which one fries the chip?
topics.post: Batteries, power banks, the 5V pin or the 3.3 pin? Pick a power source and where it connects, and see what’s safe for an ESP32-C3 SuperMini and what fries it.

topics.title: WiFi on the ESP32-C3 in 3 minutes
topics.hook: Four lines connect the board to WiFi. Here’s what to do when they don’t.
topics.post: Get an ESP32-C3 onto WiFi in four lines, then see why it fails on 5 GHz, café and wrong-password networks, and the SuperMini antenna fix.

topics.title: Bluetooth LE or WiFi: which do you need?
topics.hook: WiFi reaches the internet. BLE talks to the phone in your hand. Tick what your project needs.
topics.post: Bluetooth LE or WiFi for your ESP32-C3 project? Tick what it needs and get an answer with reasons, plus the one Bluetooth thing the C3 can’t do.

topics.title: Bluetooth LE basics: a light switch on your phone
topics.hook: Advertise, connect, then read and write a value. That’s how a phone switches an LED on.
topics.post: How does a phone switch an LED on over Bluetooth LE? Scan, connect, read, write and subscribe to an ESP32-C3 in an interactive demo.

topics.title: Why turning on WiFi resets your board
topics.hook: WiFi transmits in bursts of over 300 mA. A thin cable can’t keep up, and the board reboots.
topics.post: Board resets as soon as WiFi starts? “Brownout detector was triggered” means the voltage sagged. See why, and the cable, capacitor and power fixes.

topics.title: Deep sleep: make a battery last months
topics.hook: Asleep, the ESP32-C3 chip draws 5 microamps. Awake with WiFi, thousands of times more.
topics.post: Make an ESP32-C3 run for months on a battery: deep sleep, timer and button wake, and a calculator showing what WiFi and the power LED cost you.

topics.title: Updating your ESP32 over WiFi
topics.hook: Once the first upload is done by cable, the next ones can go over WiFi. The board keeps two copies, so a dropped update leaves the old code running.
topics.post: Update an ESP32 without plugging it in. See how over-the-air updates write into a second slot, so a dropped update leaves the old code running.

topics.title: Reading resistor color bands
topics.hook: Those colored stripes are a number. Tap the bands to change them, or type a value and see which colors it takes.
topics.post: Those colored stripes on a resistor are a number. Tap the bands and watch the value change, or type 4.7k and see its colors.

topics.title: Ohm’s law, series and parallel
topics.hook: Volts, ohms and milliamps on one small circuit. Drag the sliders and see the current, and which resistor gets too hot.
topics.post: Ohm’s law on one small circuit: drag the voltage and resistance, switch between series and parallel, and see which resistor gets too hot.

topics.title: LED basics: which way round, and why it needs a resistor
topics.hook: The long leg goes to plus. Flip the LED, pull out its resistor and change its color to see what lights and what burns.
topics.post: Which way round does an LED go, and why does it need a resistor? Flip it, pull the resistor out and change the color to see.

topics.title: Picking the resistor for an LED
topics.hook: Supply voltage, LED color and current in; the resistor out, rounded to a value you can actually buy.
topics.post: Which resistor for an LED? Pick 3.3 V or 5 V, the LED color and the current, and get a resistor you can actually buy, with its color bands.

topics.title: Capacitor types: ceramic, electrolytic and tantalum
topics.hook: What 104 means, which leg is negative, and why the voltage on the can matters.
topics.post: What does 104 on a capacitor mean? Decode any marking into pF, nF and µF, then flip an electrolytic and a tantalum to see which way round each one goes.

topics.title: How a capacitor charges through a resistor
topics.hook: Flip a switch and watch the voltage curve. R times C tells you how long it takes.
topics.post: A capacitor charging through a resistor takes about 5 × R × C to fill. Flip the switch, change R and C, and watch the curve draw itself with τ marked.

topics.title: Why every chip wants a 100 nF capacitor
topics.hook: Chips pull current in nanosecond gulps. A small capacitor right at the power pin feeds them.
topics.post: Why does every chip have a 100 nF capacitor next to it? Add one, slide it away from the power pin, and watch the supply rail dip on a scope trace.

topics.title: Switching a bigger load with a transistor
topics.hook: An ESP32 pin gives a few milliamps at 3.3 V. An NPN transistor like the 2N2222 lets that pin switch a 5 V load drawing far more. Pick the base resistor and see when it fully turns on.
topics.post: A GPIO pin can’t power a motor or a strip of lights, but it can switch a transistor that does. Pick a base resistor and watch base current, gain and Vce change live.

topics.title: Switching with a MOSFET from a 3.3 V pin
topics.hook: A logic-level MOSFET switches amps with almost no current from the pin. Pick a part and see why an IRFZ44N barely turns on at 3.3 V while an IRLZ44N or AO3400 runs cool.
topics.post: Why does an IRFZ44N barely switch from an ESP32 when an IRLZ44N works fine? Pick a MOSFET, set the gate voltage, and watch Rds(on) and the heat change.

topics.title: Flyback diodes for motors and relays
topics.hook: Switch off a relay, motor or solenoid and its coil kicks back with a voltage spike. One diode across the coil, band to the positive supply, soaks it up.
topics.post: Switch off a relay coil and the voltage at your transistor can jump far past its rating. See the spike with no diode, the right diode, and one put in backwards.

topics.title: Transistor or MOSFET: which to use
topics.hook: For a small LED or buzzer, a transistor is fine. For amps, a logic-level MOSFET. Set your load and supply and see which part fits, and why.
topics.post: Transistor or MOSFET? Set your load current and supply voltage and see which one to use with an ESP32, and how much heat each would make.

topics.title: Setting up a Raspberry Pi with no keyboard or screen
topics.hook: Raspberry Pi Imager can set the WiFi, your user and SSH before the Pi ever boots. Switch each one off and see how the Pi fails without it.
topics.post: No keyboard, no monitor? Raspberry Pi Imager sets the WiFi, a user and SSH before the first boot. Switch each setting off and see how a headless Pi fails without it.

topics.title: Why your Pi never joins the WiFi: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz
topics.hook: You flashed the card, typed the WiFi password, and the Pi never appears. If your network is 5 GHz only, a Zero 2W can’t even see it.
topics.post: You flashed the card, typed the WiFi password, and the Pi never appears. If your network is 5 GHz only, a Zero 2W can’t even see it. Pick a router and a board and see.

topics.title: Old Raspberry Pi tutorials on Bookworm: what moved
topics.hook: config.txt moved, wpa_supplicant.conf is ignored and pip install refuses. Pick a step from an old tutorial and see what it does now, and what to type instead.
topics.post: Following an older Raspberry Pi tutorial? On Bookworm, config.txt moved, wpa_supplicant.conf is ignored and pip install refuses. See each old step next to the one that works now.

topics.title: Why a Raspberry Pi slows down: under-voltage
topics.hook: Random reboots, SD card errors, WiFi dropping out. Often it isn’t the Pi: the supply or the cable can’t hold 5 V when it gets busy.
topics.post: Random reboots, SD card errors, WiFi dropping out? Your Raspberry Pi may be short of volts. Pick a supply, a cable and a load and watch the voltage sag, then decode vcgencmd get_throttled.

topics.title: Why pulling the plug corrupts a Pi’s SD card
topics.hook: Linux is always writing something. Cut the power at the wrong moment and the card can come back damaged. Shut down first, or make the card read-only.
topics.post: Pulled the plug on a Raspberry Pi and now it won’t boot? Cut the power at any moment of a file save and see what the SD card is left with, with and without the read-only overlay file system.

topics.title: A streaming speaker with Volumio
topics.hook: Plug a Pi into any speaker and anyone on the WiFi can play to it: from Spotify, an iPhone over AirPlay, or internet radio. No app accounts to share.
topics.post: Plug a Pi into any speaker and anyone on the WiFi can play to it: Spotify, AirPlay or internet radio. See which Volumio features are free and how to wire it up.

topics.title: RGB LED panels on a Pi 4: fixing flicker and garbage
topics.hook: Garbage pixels, shimmer or flicker on a HUB75 panel usually comes down to five settings. Flip them one at a time and watch the panel settle.
topics.post: Garbage pixels or flicker on an RGB LED panel driven by a Pi 4? Flip the five settings that fix it, one at a time, and watch the panel settle.

topics.title: Where’s my Pi? Finding a headless Raspberry Pi on the network
topics.hook: It booted, the light is blinking, and you have no idea what address it has. Try mypi.local, the router’s list or a scan, and see which work on your network.
topics.post: Your headless Raspberry Pi booted, but where is it? Pick your network and laptop and see whether hostname.local, the router’s device list or a scan will find it, and why guest WiFi never will.

topics.title: Zero 2W, Pi 4 or Pi 5: which Raspberry Pi for which job
topics.hook: A speaker, a sign, a desktop and a sensor on a battery all want different boards. Tick what your project needs and see which Pi fits, and why.
topics.post: Zero 2W, Pi 4 or Pi 5? Tick what your project needs, like a battery, Ethernet, 5 GHz WiFi or two screens, and see which Raspberry Pi fits and why the others don’t.

topics.title: The Raspberry Pi GPIO header: pin numbers, 3.3 V and what each pin does
topics.hook: Pin 11 is GPIO 17, the pins run at 3.3 V, and 5 V on one can kill the Pi. Tap any pin on the 40-pin header to see what it does.
topics.post: Pin 11 or GPIO 17? Tap any pin on the Raspberry Pi’s 40-pin header to see what it does, flip between physical and GPIO numbers, and see why 5 V never goes on a GPIO pin.

topics.title: Pi Zero 2W: which micro-USB port is which
topics.hook: Two micro-USB ports that look the same. One only takes power; the other is the only data port. Plug a keyboard into the wrong one and nothing happens.
topics.post: Keyboard dead on your Pi Zero 2W? Its two micro-USB ports look the same, but only one carries data. Plug a charger, keyboard, drive or DAC into each port and see what happens.

topics.title: No picture from a Pi 4: the micro-HDMI ports
topics.hook: A Pi 4 has two tiny HDMI ports, and the screen stays black more often than it should. Pick the port, the cable and when the screen comes on, and see why.
topics.post: Black screen on a Raspberry Pi 4? Two micro-HDMI ports, a monitor switched on too late, or a cable missing a wire. Pick the port, the cable and the timing and see whether you get a picture.

topics.title: Why a Pi 4 slows down when it gets hot
topics.hook: Once its chip gets too hot, a Pi 4 turns its own speed down to cool off. A bare board in a closed box can get there in a couple of minutes.
topics.post: Raspberry Pi 4 slowing down under load? Once it gets too hot it throttles itself. Pick a load and the cooling and watch ten minutes of temperature climb and the clock speed drop.
